steps.action:
# The Last Light

Maren had kept the light for thirty-one years, and in that time she had learned that the sea had moods the way people had moods — sullen gray mornings, explosive tempers, and occasionally, on certain evenings in September, a kind of silver generosity that made you forgive everything that came before.

She climbed the iron stairs each evening at dusk, one hundred and twelve steps, her right hand trailing the cold railing. She had counted them so many times the number had lost its meaning, become something more like a heartbeat — automatic, necessary, barely noticed until it stopped.

The light itself was a fourth-order Fresnel lens, installed in 1887, and Maren loved it the way she imagined surgeons loved their instruments. Precisely. Without sentimentality, but with a deep and serious respect for what it could do. On clear nights it reached fourteen miles. She knew this the way she knew her own name.

---

Her husband Thomas had come to the island with her at the beginning. He had romantic ideas about isolation, about simplicity, about what a man could become when stripped of distraction. These ideas lasted about eighteen months. One February morning she woke and found a note on the kitchen table, folded once, her name written on the outside in his careful schoolteacher's hand. She had stood there in her wool socks reading it for a long time. Then she put a pot of coffee on, climbed the stairs, and made sure the light was clean.

She did not hate him for leaving. The island asked something of a person, and not everyone had it to give. She had tried to explain this to her sister over the radio once — that staying was not stubbornness, not loneliness glorified, but rather a particular calling, like a note only certain ears could hear. Her sister said, *Maren, that's the saddest thing I've ever heard.* Maren had laughed, and the laugh had surprised them both.

---

The winter she turned fifty-four, a vessel called the *Aldric Star* went into trouble three miles off the point. It was February, a storm that had come faster than the forecasts suggested, the kind of storm that reminded you the sea had no obligation to be predictable. Maren was in the lantern room when she saw the lights listing badly. She had already radioed the coast guard. She had already done everything she could do. And yet she stood there with her hands against the cold glass, watching.

The light turned. The beam swept out across the black water. It did not save the ship — the coast guard did that, pulled eleven men from the water in inflatable survival suits, all of them alive, one of them barely. But afterward, one of the crew, a young deckhand named Piotr, came to thank her in person, took the ferry out and hiked up the gravel path to her door.

He was perhaps twenty-two, still waterlogged-looking even days later, his eyes carrying the specific expression of someone who had recently understood what mortality meant in a physical sense.

She made him coffee and they sat at her small table.

"You kept the light on," he said.

"That's the job," she told him.

He nodded, but she could see he wanted it to mean more than that, wanted her to say something large and consoling about hope, about the human will to guide one another through the dark. She understood the impulse. She had felt it herself once, had wrapped her purpose in that kind of language.

But she had come to believe that the grandeur was actually in the plainness of it. *That's the job.* Someone has to stand in the high place and keep the light burning so that others can know where the rocks are. You do this every night regardless of whether ships are passing, regardless of whether anyone will ever know you did it. You do it because the alternative — the dark, the silence, the rocks unmarked — is worse. Not dramatically worse. Just worse, in the steady, accumulated way that neglect is always worse than attention.

She did not say all of this to Piotr. He was young and had almost drowned and deserved a simpler afternoon.

She refilled his coffee and they looked out the window at the water, which today was calm and almost gentle, as if it had no memory of what it had done.

---

In the spring, the Coast Guard Auxiliary sent a letter informing her that the station was being automated. It was something she had known was coming — other lights had gone the same way, one by one, the keepers let go, the mechanisms upgraded, the old human presence replaced with sensors and timers and systems that didn't need coffee or wool socks or thirty-one years of learning the sea's particular moods.

She read the letter twice, folded it, and put it in the drawer where she kept important papers.

That evening she climbed the stairs — one hundred and twelve steps — and cleaned the lens with the soft cloth she kept on the hook by the door. She polished each prism carefully. She checked the mechanism. She wound what needed winding.

Outside, the sun was going down in long red streaks across the water, and she stood for a while just watching it, this sea she had given her life to, this stretch of gray and green and black that had taken her husband and her youth and her appetite for elsewhere, and had given her back something harder and quieter and more durable, something she did not have a word for yet and suspected she never would.

The light came on.

It swept out across the water, same as it had for a hundred and thirty years. Fourteen miles, on a clear night. Enough to show a ship where the rocks were. Enough to say: *here is the danger, here is the edge, go carefully.*

Maren stood in the lantern room and watched the light go out and come back, go out and come back. She stayed until it was full dark and the stars were out and she had counted the rhythm of the beam seventeen times without meaning to.

Then she went downstairs and made dinner for one, the same as always, and listened to the water, and was not unhappy.
